hub.description: Decks and fences for Chattanooga homes on ridge and valley lots, planned around the slope of the yard and where storm water runs across it.
hub.intro: Most yards in Chattanooga are not flat. Homes sit on the sides of Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge, and plenty of valley lots still fall toward a creek or the Tennessee River. Chattanooga also gets a lot of rain. Put those together and the first questions on a Chattanooga deck or fence are about slope and water, not boards and stain. We want to know where runoff crosses your yard and how far the ground drops from the house to the back line. Below is how each of those plays out for a deck and for a fence.

sections.heading: Why slope and rain lead the plan in Chattanooga
paragraphs: Chattanooga sits in Southeast Tennessee, where the Tennessee River cuts between long ridges. That setting gives many houses a walkout basement or a back door well above the grass. Plenty of side yards climb toward the neighbor, too. Each of those changes the work. A deck on a slope needs taller posts and more bracing. Fence panels have to step down or tilt to follow the ground. When a hard storm comes through, water moves across these lots fast, so footings and post holes have to sit where runoff will not wash the soil out from around them.

sections.heading: Decks on Chattanooga hillsides
paragraphs: On a lot that drops away behind the house, a deck is often the only flat outdoor space you have. In Chattanooga, that is common on Missionary Ridge and in parts of Hixson. A raised deck there puts more load on each post, so footing size and bracing matter more than they would on a low deck in a flat yard. Stairs matter too. A long run of steps has to land on solid ground that will not wash out after a few storms. Our [deck builder page for Chattanooga](/deck-builder-chattanooga-tn/) goes further into footings in rock and what the codes office will want to see.

sections.heading: Fences that follow the ground
paragraphs: A fence line in Chattanooga rarely runs level from one corner to the next. On a gentle grade the panels can rack, meaning the rails tilt to match the slope. A steeper one usually calls for sections that step down like stairs, which leaves triangle gaps at the bottom that may need filling if you have a dog. Rock is the other surprise. Post holes on the ridges around Chattanooga often hit stone before they reach full depth. Our [fence company page for Chattanooga](/fence-company-chattanooga-tn/) covers that in detail, and the [guide to fencing a sloped yard](/guides/fence-on-a-slope/) explains stepped and racked panels.

sections.heading: Who reviews your project
paragraphs: Before anything gets built, sort out whose rules apply. Addresses inside city limits go through the City of Chattanooga. Homes outside Chattanooga city limits, in unincorporated parts of Hamilton County, fall under the county instead. Homes inside the town of Lookout Mountain answer to that town. Permit rules and fence placement rules can differ between these offices, so confirm with the right one before you settle on a plan.

Two other layers can apply. Some older Chattanooga neighborhoods sit in local historic districts, where a deck or fence that can be seen from the street may need design review before a permit. Many newer Chattanooga subdivisions, especially out toward East Brainerd, have HOAs with their own approval process for fence style and deck placement. Neither one replaces the permit. If you have a date in mind, plan for both.

sections.heading: Getting started on a Chattanooga estimate
paragraphs: A rough idea is enough to begin. When you fill out the [estimate form](#estimate), use the notes box to tell us how steep the yard is and where water collects after a storm. If you already have a property survey, say so, and mention any HOA. Want both a deck and a fence? Tell us in the same request, since deck stairs and fence gates often need to be planned together on a sloped Chattanooga lot.

faqs.q: Should I build the deck or the fence first on a sloped Chattanooga lot?
faqs.a: It depends on access. If the deck sits high off a hillside, materials usually have to come around the side of the house, and a finished fence can get in the way. On the other hand, a fence that has to hold in a dog may not be able to wait. In many cases the deck goes first and the fence follows, with a gate placed near where the deck stairs land. Tell us about both projects together so the two plans fit.

faqs.q: How does heavy rain in Chattanooga affect a new deck or fence?
faqs.a: In Chattanooga, rain is one of the main things working against a deck or fence. Water running across a slope can wash soil away from footings and posts over time. Standing water against wood keeps it damp and invites rot. So downspouts should not empty onto footings, and the concrete around posts should be crowned so it sheds water. A fence that crosses a runoff path needs room at the bottom for water to pass.

faqs.q: What should I know about building on Lookout Mountain?
faqs.a: Start with who governs your address. If you live inside the town of Lookout Mountain, the town sets the rules. Other parts of the mountain fall under other local governments, and the mountain continues south into Georgia. After that, expect rock. Many lots up top have stone close to the surface, which affects footings and post holes. Access can matter too, since some driveways there are steep and tight for a loaded trailer.

deck.description: Deck builder for Chattanooga hillside homes. Raised decks and long stairs planned for rock on the ridges and wet red clay in the valleys.
deck.intro: In Chattanooga, a lot of back doors open a full story or more above the yard. Plenty of houses on Missionary Ridge and in Hixson were built into a slope, and the deck is often the only level place to sit outside. Building on that kind of lot is a different job from putting a low deck on flat ground. Posts get taller and each footing carries more weight. Rain running down the hill will find any soft spot around a footing, so drainage gets planned alongside the framing. When you talk to any deck builder about a lot like yours, ask how they will handle both.

sections.heading: Raised decks on Chattanooga slopes
paragraphs: On a tall Chattanooga deck, most of the work is in the parts underneath. Longer posts need bracing so the deck does not sway when people move across it. Beam and joist sizes depend on how far each piece spans. The connection to the house has to be bolted and flashed so water does not get behind the rim board. None of that shows much once the boards are down, but it decides whether a raised deck stays solid for a long time or starts to loosen.

The space under a high deck is worth thinking about early. Some owners want it dry for storage or a patio, which means planning a way to carry water off the deck above. Others leave it open and want it to look tidy from the yard. Stairs are the other big decision. On a steep Chattanooga lot, a long straight run may land in a spot that stays muddy, so a landing or a turn can put the bottom step on better ground.

sections.heading: Footings in rock and clay
paragraphs: Ground conditions around Chattanooga change a lot over a short distance. Up on the ridges, footing holes often hit rock before they reach the depth the inspector wants. Down in the valleys, the soil is often a dense red clay that holds water after a storm. Rock may mean drilling, or moving a post over a little so it lands on better ground. When neither works, the codes office can tell you what it will accept. With clay, the main job is keeping water away from the footing so the soil around it does not soften.

Footing depth and size are not something to guess at from a photo. Those numbers come from the code your local office follows and from what the inspector sees in the open hole. On a hillside deck in Chattanooga, tall posts and long stairs each need solid footings of their own, and every one of them should sit on undisturbed soil or rock. In newer East Brainerd subdivisions, part of a back yard may be fill that was pushed there during grading, and a footing should go through it rather than rest on it.

sections.heading: Keeping water away from the deck
paragraphs: A lot of deck trouble in Chattanooga starts with water, not with the boards. Downspouts that empty right beside a post keep the soil soft and can slowly wash it out. A gutter that overflows onto the deck keeps one edge of the boards wet. Where the deck meets the house, flashing over the ledger keeps rain from soaking framing you cannot see. Before footings are laid out, it pays to look at where the roof water goes and move any downspout that points at the new work.

Big storms in Chattanooga also move soil. On a slope, the ground right below a deck can start to erode once grass stops growing in the shade under it. A bed of gravel or a shallow swale can keep that soil in place. If water already cuts a path across your yard every time it storms, tell us. It is much easier to plan the deck around a known runoff path than to fix a washed out footing later.

sections.heading: Boards that handle shade and humidity
paragraphs: Many Chattanooga lots are heavily wooded, especially on the ridges. That shade is welcome in July, but it keeps a deck damp longer after rain, and damp wood grows mildew and moss. Pressure treated pine handles it well if you clean it and reseal it on a regular schedule. Composite boards resist rot better, but they can still grow mildew in shade and need washing. The framing under a composite deck is usually still treated wood, so drainage matters either way.

View lots are the exception. A deck on a cleared view lot on Lookout Mountain or Missionary Ridge may get full afternoon sun, and darker composite boards often get hotter underfoot than wood. If you are choosing between materials, our [comparison of wood and composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) walks through upkeep and surface heat in Tennessee weather.

sections.heading: Permits and approvals for a Chattanooga deck
paragraphs: Attached and raised decks usually need a building permit, and on a hillside lot nearly every deck is raised. Your address decides which office handles it. The City of Chattanooga covers homes inside city limits. Hamilton County covers unincorporated areas outside any city. The town of Lookout Mountain handles its own. Ask your deck builder who will pull the permit, and confirm the process with the office that covers your lot. Our [guide to deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains how inspections usually work.

Two more approvals can come before the permit. If your home is in one of Chattanooga's local historic districts, a deck that can be seen from the street may need design review. In a subdivision with an HOA, which is common in East Brainerd, the architectural committee may want to see a drawing and the materials before they sign off. Both can take a while, so send those requests before you pick a start date.

sections.heading: Decks near the river and Chickamauga Lake
paragraphs: Some Chattanooga decks are built to face the water. On the North Shore, some homes look toward the Tennessee River and downtown. In Hixson, some lots back up to Chickamauga Lake or one of its coves. On the lake, TVA owns or controls land along much of the shoreline, and work near the water line may need TVA approval as well as a local permit. Check both before you settle on a design. When you are ready, send the basics through the [estimate form](#estimate) and note how close the deck would sit to the water.

faqs.q: How deep do deck footings go in Chattanooga?
faqs.a: There is no single answer. Depth is set by the office that issues your permit, and the ground itself can change the plan, since a ridge lot and a valley lot rarely behave the same. The inspector usually checks footing holes before concrete goes in, and on rocky ground they may have specific requirements. On clay, the bigger worry is keeping water away from the footing once it is poured.

faqs.q: Can you build a deck on a very steep lot in Hixson or on Missionary Ridge?
faqs.a: A steep lot does not usually rule out a deck, but it changes the job. It calls for taller posts and more bracing, and it can take longer to carry materials from the driveway to the back of the house. Sometimes the better plan is a smaller deck at door level with stairs down to a lower landing, instead of one big platform on very tall posts. The slope needs to be seen in person before choosing either one.

faqs.q: How do I keep a shaded deck in Chattanooga from getting slick?
faqs.a: Shade and humidity let mildew and algae form on wood and composite alike. Wash the surface a couple of times a year with a cleaner made for your decking, and sweep off leaves before they mat down. Trimming low branches lets in more light and air, which helps the boards dry after rain. On a wood deck, many sealers include mildew protection that helps between washings.

faqs.q: Do I need HOA approval for a deck in East Brainerd?
faqs.a: If your home is in a subdivision with an HOA, you probably do. Many of the newer subdivisions in East Brainerd have covenants that cover exterior changes, decks included. Read your covenants first, then ask the committee what it needs to see. A simple drawing showing size and placement is a common starting point. HOA approval is separate from the permit, so you may need both before work begins.

faqs.q: What if my lot near the Tennessee River is in a flood zone?
faqs.a: It does not always rule out a deck, but it can change the rules. The codes office for your Chattanooga address may have requirements for building in a mapped flood zone, such as how the deck is anchored and whether anything can be enclosed underneath. Look up your lot on the flood maps or ask the office before the design is settled.

fence.description: Fence installation in Chattanooga for sloped yards. Privacy fences that step down steep grades and let storm water pass under the bottom boards.
fence.intro: Few fence lines in Chattanooga cross flat ground. A backyard in East Brainerd may fall toward a drainage ditch, while a lot on Missionary Ridge can drop sharply from the house to the back line. That slope is what makes fence installation here harder than on a flat lot. Panels have to step down or rack to follow the grade, and post holes on the ridges often run into rock. Storm water also has to get past the bottom of the fence without washing the soil out. This page covers what to plan for on that kind of ground.

sections.heading: Stepped or racked fence lines in Chattanooga
paragraphs: There are two ways to run a fence down a hill. A racked fence tilts its rails to follow the ground, so the bottom stays close to the soil the whole way. With a stepped fence, each section stays level and drops at every post, like a staircase. Racking looks smooth on a steady, gentle grade. Stepping works better on steep or uneven ground, which describes a lot of Chattanooga yards, but it leaves a triangle of open space under each section.

Those gaps matter if you have a dog or want real privacy. They can be closed with a bottom board cut to the slope, or with soil and gravel brought up along the line where drainage allows. Some yards use both methods, racking where the grade is gentle and stepping where it drops off. The [guide to fencing a sloped yard](/guides/fence-on-a-slope/) compares the two and shows how each one changes gate placement.

sections.heading: Setting posts in rocky Chattanooga ground
paragraphs: Posts decide how long a fence stays straight. On Lookout Mountain and along the ridges, post holes often hit rock partway down. When that happens, the options are to break through it with heavier equipment or to shift the post slightly so it lands in a softer spot. Shifting a post changes the spacing of the panels on either side, so we would rather know about rock early than discover it on install day. If you have dug in your yard before, tell us what you found.

Valley lots bring a different problem. Red clay holds water, and a post sitting in wet clay can lean over time as the soil moves. Concrete helps, but only if the top is shaped to shed rain away from the wood instead of letting water collect around the post. On the wettest parts of a yard, a layer of gravel at the bottom of the hole gives water somewhere to drain.

sections.heading: Runoff and the bottom of your fence
paragraphs: Chattanooga storms can send a lot of water across a yard at once. A solid privacy fence built straight across that path acts like a small dam. Leaves and mulch pile up against the boards, water backs up behind them, and the bottom rail stays wet long enough to rot. The fix is usually simple. Leave a gap under the fence where water crosses, or run the line so it follows the flow instead of blocking it. Walk your yard during the next hard rain and note where water goes.

Newer subdivisions around Chattanooga often have drainage easements along back or side lot lines. Depending on the easement terms, a fence there may be restricted, or you may have to take it down if the easement ever needs work. Your plat or HOA documents should show where they are. If a creek or wet weather ditch runs through the lot, ask the City of Chattanooga or Hamilton County whether any stream buffer rules apply before you pick the line.

sections.heading: Privacy fences on a hillside lot
paragraphs: On flat ground, a privacy fence blocks the view in both directions. A Chattanooga slope can change that. If your neighbor's house sits uphill, they may still see over a fence at the bottom of your yard. Placing the fence higher on the grade, closer to the patio or deck you want to screen, usually does more than running it along the lowest property line. Height limits vary by jurisdiction and by HOA, so ask before you plan a taller section.

Style matters on a slope too. Board on board gives full coverage from both sides, which helps when the uphill neighbor looks down on the back of your fence. Ridge lots with open views can catch more wind than sheltered valley yards, and a solid fence takes the full push of it. Stronger posts and closer post spacing help. A design with small gaps between boards also lets wind through, if you can accept a little less privacy.

sections.heading: Property lines, permits, and HOAs in Chattanooga
paragraphs: Start with where your lines really are. Hillside lots in Chattanooga can have odd shapes, and an old fence or tree line is not always the boundary. A survey or located corner pins give you something solid to build from. Before anyone digs, a call to Tennessee 811 gets buried utility lines marked, so ask your fence company who will place that request. Our guide to [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) covers surveys and talking with neighbors.

Whether a fence needs a permit, and where it can sit on the lot, depends on which office covers your address. That may be the City of Chattanooga or Hamilton County. Homes inside the town of Lookout Mountain follow the town. In a local historic district, a fence that faces the street may need design review first. HOAs in East Brainerd and other newer areas often decide the style and which side of the fence faces out.

sections.heading: Gates and dogs on sloped yards
paragraphs: On a sloped Chattanooga yard, gates are where most of the trouble shows up. A gate that swings downhill clears the ground easily, but one that swings uphill can drag partway open. The best spot for a gate is usually the flattest stretch of the line, or a spot where the ground at the opening can be leveled. For dogs, the gate should close and latch on its own, and the gap under it should stay small as the posts settle. If the gate opens near deck stairs, our [deck builder page for Chattanooga](/deck-builder-chattanooga-tn/) talks about where those stairs should land.

faqs.q: Can a privacy fence follow a steep yard in Chattanooga?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. On a steep grade the fence is usually stepped, with each section kept level and dropped at the post. That keeps the boards plumb and the fence looking square, but it leaves gaps at the bottom that you may want to close. On gentler ground, racking the panels keeps the bottom tight to the soil. Where the grade changes along the line, a fence can switch from one method to the other.

faqs.q: Is cedar or pressure treated pine better for a fence in Chattanooga weather?
faqs.a: Both can work. Cedar resists rot on its own and tends to stay straighter as it dries. Pressure treated pine usually costs less and takes stain well once it has dried out. In a damp, shaded yard, the posts matter more than the pickets. Posts rated for ground contact and set so water drains away are what keep the fence standing. Pairing treated posts with cedar boards is a common approach.

faqs.q: Do I need a survey before fence installation in Chattanooga?
faqs.a: It is not always required, but it is the safest start. On hillside lots, the property line often does not follow the tree line or an old fence. If your corner pins are still in the ground and you can find them, that may be enough. Otherwise, a surveyor can locate them. A fence on the wrong side of the line can lead to a dispute with a neighbor, and moving a finished fence usually costs more than a survey.

faqs.q: How do I keep my dog from getting under a fence on a slope?
faqs.a: Dogs that dig tend to go for the low corners of a stepped fence. Closing those triangles with a bottom board cut to the grade helps a lot, and some owners add a strip of gravel along the base. Check the fence line after big storms, because runoff on a Chattanooga hillside can scour a new gap under the boards where there was none before.

faqs.q: How far ahead should I plan a fence in an East Brainerd HOA?
faqs.a: Leave room for the architectural committee. Many HOAs review requests on a set schedule and want a drawing that shows the fence line and style before they approve it. Once you have approval, the permit, if one is required, is a separate step. Start the HOA request before you choose an install date. You can still send us the details through the [estimate form](#estimate) while you wait.
